title: What a good intro call should decide
metaTitle: What a good intro call should decide
excerpt: A useful intro call ends with fit, a rough shape of the work, and a yes or no on writing a proposal. It is a decision meeting, not a free strategy workshop.
alt: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table. The setup is a working conversation, the scale of an intro call rather than a workshop.
caption: A short call should end with a decision. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How long should an intro call be?
faqs.answer: Half an hour is enough to test fit, sketch the shape of the work, and decide whether a proposal is worth writing. Hanabi uses a 30-minute intro. If the idea needs a workshop, that is a separate engagement with a scope, not something to extract from the first call.

faqs.question: What should I bring to the call?
faqs.answer: Bring who the site is for, the one action it should earn, and what already exists, whether that is a URL, a name, or a product in use. Three references help more than a long deck. If you have a hard date, say it, and if you do not, say that too.

faqs.question: What if the studio is not a fit?
faqs.answer: End the call there. A clear no saves both sides a proposal nobody should write. Ask what kind of partner would fit if they know, and thank them for the limit. A proposal written out of politeness becomes a project with the wrong brief.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A design studio intro call should end with three decisions: whether there is a fit, the rough shape of the work, and whether a proposal is worth writing. It should not become a free strategy workshop.

Half an hour is the right size for that. Hanabi books the intro as a 30-minute call. You spend it on the offer, the constraint, and the edge of the job. You do not spend it designing the homepage live, naming the product, or rebuilding the business model. Those are projects. The call is the gate in front of them.

## What fit means

Fit is mutual, and it should be said out loud before anyone talks about price.

The studio is a fit when the work matches what they actually do. For Hanabi that means websites, brand systems, ecommerce, and product interfaces for founders and small teams, designed and built in one place. A project that is only a logo, only a pitch deck, or a full product organization is a different partner. Saying so on the call is a successful call.

You are a fit when you can name a buyer and a next step. “We sell a small-batch good to people who already care about the material” is enough to start. “We want to be the platform for everything” is not a brief. The studio should be able to repeat your offer back in a sentence. If they cannot, either the offer is still too foggy or they were not listening. Both are reasons to pause.

Fit includes temperament. You want plain updates and a process that can change when the offer changes. The studio wants a person who can approve. If the call reveals that six people must agree and none of them is in the room, the schedule you imagine is not real yet. Name the approver before a proposal pretends otherwise.

## The rough shape of the work

Shape is not a full scope. It is a paragraph both sides recognize.

For a marketing site, the paragraph is the set of pages, the one action the site should earn, and what must not change. For a shop, it is whether you are migrating a catalog, what has to keep working at checkout, and which parts of the old theme you are willing to leave. For a product interface, it is the one workflow that should feel finished, including the empty state and the error.

Leave the field list, the component inventory, and the animation ideas for later. If the call spends twenty minutes on a nav label, it has slipped into production. Park the label. Return to the shape.

A useful test for a homepage, when the project is a site, comes from how little time a stranger will give you. Nielsen Norman Group’s [research on page visits](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/), published in 2011, found that the first ten seconds are when someone is most likely to leave, and that a clear value proposition in that window is what earns a longer stay. You do not design that sentence on the intro call. You do decide whether the project’s job includes it. If the founder wants a poetic line and also wants a stranger to understand the product, the shape of the work includes both, in that order: the line, then the sentence that answers what this is and how to talk to a person.

Dates belong in the shape as constraints, not as decoration. A conference, a shipment, a fundraise. If the date cannot move, the scope must. The call should say which one bends. A proposal that promises both an immovable date and an unknown scope is a proposal written too early.

## Whether a proposal is worth writing

A proposal costs time on both sides. Write one when the fit is real and the shape is stable enough to price. Decline when the project is still a cloud, when the studio is the wrong tool, or when the approver is missing.

The close of the call can be three sentences.

- We are a fit, or we are not, and why.
- The work looks like this slice, with this edge.
- We will write a proposal, or we will not.

If the answer is yes, say what the proposal will cover and what it will assume. If the answer is no, stop. A “let us send something anyway” produces a document nobody can accept, then a trail of revisions that are really a second discovery. Politeness is not a scope.

Price can be a range if the studio knows the shape well enough. A false precision is worse than a range. “This is a marketing site of about this many pages, and the range looks like this, assuming we get access and copy” is an honest end. A single number pulled from a template, before anyone has seen the current site, will be renegotiated. Say the assumptions instead.

You should leave knowing the next message: a proposal by a named day, a request for one missing fact, or a no. “We’ll be in touch” is not a decision.

## What the call is not

It is not a critique of your current site unless a single example unlocks the shape. One URL, one problem, then back to the decision. A screen-share tour of every page is a workshop.

It is not a branding exercise. If you only have a name, the project may include identity. The call decides that it does. It does not pick the typeface.

It is not a technical audit. Stack questions matter when they change the shape: a shop that must keep its URLs, a product that must live in an existing repo, a team that must edit without a developer. Note them. Do not spend the half hour in the inspector.

It is not free consulting you can hand to another builder. A studio that thinks clearly will say useful things. Those things are there to test fit. Taking a full information architecture from an unpaid call, then hiring someone else to execute it, is a good way to get a shallow version of a conversation that was never the work.

## How to use the half hour

A simple split keeps the call honest.

1. Ten minutes on the company: who it is for, what you sell, what has to be true after launch.
2. Ten minutes on the shape: pages or flows, what exists, what must survive, the date if there is one.
3. Ten minutes on fit and the next step: who does the work, what you will own, whether a proposal gets written.

Send the current URL the day before if you have one. If the studio cannot open it, you have already learned something about the call. Bring the person who can approve, or say you cannot. A proxy who must “check with the founder” can listen. They cannot close.

Take notes in their words. The shape you both repeat at the end is the shape the proposal must match. If the proposal later describes a different project, you are allowed to say so. The call was the agreement about what the paper is for.

Before that call, a little preparation removes the stalls. The list is short, and it is the next piece: [what to have ready before kickoff](/blog/what-to-prepare-before-kickoff). Read it even if kickoff is still a few weeks away. The same gaps waste the intro.

When you want that half hour with Hanabi, [book an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Come with the offer and the constraint. Leave with a fit, a shape, and a decision on a proposal.
